I always help out with the Sunday potlucks down in the fellowship hall. I like to be useful, you know, making sure everyone gets a plate and the tables look nice. But lately, I... I keep doing these odd things, and it's getting so folks are starting to whisper and stare at me.

I just held it up and I didn't move at all. I was just stuck there, holding this spoon up high like a statue, and people were standing right there with their paper plates waiting on me to serve them, and I just couldn't seem to move my arm to scoop a single thing.

Over and over and over again. I'd fold them in half, smooth the edges down, and then just keep folding that exact same stack while a whole line of hungry people were backing up all the way to the double doors, just waiting on me to set them down so they could get their dessert. Well, no, I... I wouldn't say it's a worry. Not a worry at all, really. It's not like I'm standing there fretting over something terrible happening if I don't fold 'em, or hearing some voice telling me I got to do it. Lord knows I got enough real things to worry about in this life, but right in those moments? No. It's exactly like you said—it's like I just freeze up.

And with them thick paper napkins, it was the exact same way. I wasn't thinking, "Oh, I need to fold these so the corners match up perfect," or worrying about them being dirty. I just... my hands just kept moving, smoothing 'em down, over and over, and my brain was just completely out to pasture. I didn't even feel upset or worried until I sort of came to my senses and saw that whole line of folks backed up to the double doors staring at me like I'd grown a second head. That's when the worry hits, Doctor, the sheer embarrassment of it all, having everybody looking at you like you're crazy. But during the actual doing of it? No, no thoughts at all. Just completely frozen up like a deer in the headlights, without a single reason why.

Well, I certainly don't see anything that isn't there, thank the Lord, and I don't hear any voices or anything spooky like that. My mind is quiet in that regard. Folks just look at me like they can't find what I'm saying at all. They just stare at me, trying to piece it together, and I'm standing there realizing my mouth is just running from one thing to another without a lick of sense to connect 'em. It makes me feel terribly confused, Doctor, because in my head I mean to answer straight, but what comes out is just a whole mess of beans and hymns and garden flowers, and it just leaves everybody scratching their heads.

I don't know why I just get stuck doing these strange things when I'm just trying to do my part and help out.\n\nDoctor: When you're standing there folding the napkins over and over, or holding the spoon up and can't move, are you aware of any worried thought or urge telling you that you have to keep doing it, or does it feel more like your body just freezes up without any particular thought pushing you to do it?\n\nPatient: Well, no, I... I wouldn't say it's a worry. Not a worry at all, really. It's not like I'm standing there fretting over something terrible happening if I don't fold 'em, or hearing some voice telling me I got to do it. Not one thought in my head. My arm just went up and stayed up, like it turned to heavy stone right there on the fellowship hall linoleum. I could see the people, you know? I could see Mr. Henderson looking at me with his little paper plate, just waiting for his scoop, but there was no thought pushing me to hold it there. Just... nothing. Just stuck. \n\nAnd with them thick paper napkins, it was the exact same way. I wasn't thinking, \"Oh, I need to fold these so the corners match up perfect,\" or worrying about them being dirty. I just... my hands just kept moving, smoothing 'em down, over and over, and my brain was just completely out to pasture. I didn't even feel upset or worried until I sort of came to my senses and saw that whole line of folks backed up to the double doors staring at me like I'd grown a second head. That's when the worry hits, Doctor, the sheer embarrassment of it all, having everybody looking at you like you're crazy. But during the actual doing of it? No, no thoughts at all. I know some folks my age are always in and out of the doctor's office, falling down and hitting their heads and what have you. Like my neighbor, Mr. Abernathy, he took a tumble off his porch steps just last November and had a terrible bump on his head, but me? No, I'm real careful. I always hold onto the handrail when I go down the steps to the basement to fetch my canning jars. Never hit my head, never had any of those... well, you called them neurological things. My memory and all that has always been just fine, except for these awful freezing up spells I just told you about. \n\nAnd as for pills and such, well, I just take my same water pill for my blood pressure that Dr. Miller prescribed me... oh, it must be five or six years ago now. He gave me one of those plastic organizers, you know the ones, with the days of the week printed on 'em in big black letters, so I never miss a day. Sunday, Monday, right on down the line. I keep it right next to the toaster so I see it when I make my morning tea. But he hasn't changed it, hasn't added anything new at all. I don't take anything else. And then someone mentioned choir practice, because we're doing that big cantata soon and everyone is getting their schedules sorted out. Well, I meant to answer them just as straight as an arrow. I knew exactly what I wanted to say about the yarn I bought at the five-and-dime. \n\nBut when I opened my mouth, my words just... they just ran off. They ran off completely. I started talking about the green beans I was putting up in jars, and then somehow that turned into talking about the hymns we sang last Sunday, and before I knew it, I was going on and on about the aphids on my yellow roses out by the back fence. He gave me one of those plastic organizers, you know the ones, with the days of the week printed on 'em in big black letters, so I never miss a day. Sunday, Monday, right on down the line. I keep it right next to the toaster so I see it when I make my morning tea. But he hasn't changed it, hasn't added anything new at all. I don't take anything else. I certainly don't drink any alcohol or take any kind of bad substances—my father smoked a pipe when I was little and the smell of it was enough to put me off even tobacco for my whole life. \n\nSo no, no new medicines, no sicknesses, no falling down. I'm just healthy as a horse, which makes it all the more confounding why my arm would just stick up in the air over that macaroni salad like that. It just doesn't make a single lick of sense to me, Doctor, it really doesn't.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any other changes lately, like hearing or seeing things that others don't, having thoughts or beliefs that others find strange, or feeling unusually sad, anxious, or confused?\n\nPatient: Well, I certainly don't see anything that isn't there, thank the Lord, and I don't hear any voices or anything spooky like that. My mind is quiet in that regard. And I wouldn't say I'm sad, exactly, just terribly embarrassed like I mentioned before. But you asked about feeling confused, or folks finding things strange, and... well, there is one other thing that's been bothering me lately, now that you bring it up. It's my talking, Doctor. \n\nIt happens when I'm just trying to have a regular conversation. Like just the other day, the ladies at the church—Mrs. Higgins and Betty, you know, Betty always wears those big floral hats and sits right in the third pew—they were asking me about the new prayer blankets we're knitting for the winter drive. And then someone mentioned choir practice, because we're doing that big cantata soon and everyone is getting their schedules sorted out. Well, I meant to answer them just as straight as an arrow. I knew exactly what I wanted to say about the yarn I bought at the five-and-dime. \n\nBut when I opened my mouth, my words just... they just ran off. They ran off completely. I started talking about the green beans I was putting up in jars, and then somehow that turned into talking about the hymns we sang last Sunday, and before I knew it, I was going on and on about the aphids on my yellow roses out by the back fence. I don't even know how I got from prayer blankets to green beans to my roses! \n\nAnd I could see it right there on their faces. Betty just tilted her head, and Mrs. Higgins got this squinty look, like she was trying to read a map upside down. Folks just look at me like they can't find what I'm saying at all. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, my energy is just fine, Doctor, and my mood... well, I wouldn't say I'm depressed or anything like that. I still love my garden, I really do. Just being out there with the dirt and the Lord's earth, it's a real comfort to me. But... well, as for the church activities, that's a whole different kettle of fish right now. 

I've actually had to... well, I've had to step back from some of my choir and church volunteering lately. And it breaks my heart, it truly does, because I've been singing alto in that choir since Reverend Thomas was preaching, and that's got to be going on twenty years now. I've always been the one to help organize the socials and the drives. But it’s just gotten to where I can't seem to keep things straight anymore. I just mix up the plans, you see. Completely scramble them up in my head. 

Like just a few weeks ago, I was supposed to be in charge of organizing the donation boxes for the winter drive—putting the canned goods in one pile and the dry goods in another, making sure the expiration dates were good, just simple things I've done a hundred times. And I don't know what happened, but I had everything all jumbled up with the Sunday school supplies and the old hymnals we were supposed to be sending out to be rebound. I was telling people to put the green beans with the chalk! 

And folks... well, people get uncomfortable. I can see it in their eyes, just like when my words run away from me. They don't want to say anything mean to me, being good Christian folks, but they get that tight little smile, and they start shifting from one foot to the other. And then poor Betty or Mrs. Higgins ends up having to stay late and completely redo what I was supposed to handle. They have to go behind my back and sort it all out all over again, fixing the schedules I mixed up or the boxes I packed wrong. 

So I just told them, I said, "Maybe I just need to take a little break for a while." It's not that I don't have the interest, Doctor, or that I don't want to be there, because I really do. I miss it terribly. But it's just too hard knowing I'm making a mess of the plans and making folks feel awkward, and causing all that extra work for everybody else. It just seemed better to stay out of their way.

Well, no, Doctor, it's not a memory thing, not at all. I know I just said I get the church plans all mixed up in my head, but that's entirely different from forgetting, you see. My memory is sharp as a tack. I really haven't had any trouble remembering what folks tell me or when I'm supposed to be somewhere.

I have this lovely little wall calendar hanging right by the rotary telephone in the kitchen—the bank gives them out every year right around Thanksgiving, you know the ones, they always have those sweet little kittens sitting in woven baskets or playing with balls of yarn? Well, I write every single thing down on that calendar with my red pen. I knew I had to be right here to see you today at 2:15, and I was sitting out there in your waiting room by two o'clock on the dot. 

And as for conversations, well, I remember exactly what people tell me. I don't go repeating myself or asking the same things over and over like a broken record, no sir. Just this past Tuesday, I was talking to Mr. Henderson—he's our postman, drives that little white truck with the blue eagle on the side—and he told me his daughter just had her second baby. A little girl named Sarah, seven pounds and four ounces, born at the county hospital. I remembered to ask him how she was doing because he'd told me way back in the spring that she was due in late October, and I kept that right up here in my head all those months. 

So no, I don't forget what folks tell me. It's just... well, like I said, it's the getting my own words out straight and scrambling up the sorting boxes that's the problem. But remembering the actual information? No, my mind holds onto all that just as clear as a bell.

Well now, let me sit and chew on that for a second, Doctor. You know, time has a funny way of slipping by when you get to be my age, it just runs right through your fingers like dry potting soil. But no, it certainly wasn't an overnight thing. I didn't just wake up on a Tuesday morning with my tongue all tied in knots and my hands putting the canned corn in with the choir robes. But it hasn't been years and years, either, thank goodness. 

If I really trace it back... back to when folks first started getting that confused look on their faces, and when I first started realizing my words were just running clean away from me... I'd say it's been right about six months now. Yes, half a year. I know that for a fact because it was right around the time we were getting ready for the Easter sunrise service. We had that terrible late frost that just about ruined all the dogwood blooms, and I was out in the front yard trying to cover my delicate azaleas with some old bedsheets—the blue striped ones my sister Martha gave me back in the late nineties, they're terribly worn at the hems now but they do the trick for the frost. 

Anyway, Mrs. Higgins had walked over to the fence to ask if I'd ordered the palm fronds for Palm Sunday. And I remember standing there, holding a corner of that blue sheet, and I opened my mouth to tell her I'd already called the florist down on Main Street. But out came this whole long string of nonsense about the recipe for my paprika deviled eggs and the price of the white shoe polish I use on my Sunday heels! That was the very first time she gave me that squinty, upside-down-map look I was telling you about. 

So yes, all this odd behavior, the muddling things up at the church and the hard-to-follow talking... it hasn't been forever, but it’s been noticeable for about the past six months now. Six months of just... well, just making a mess of my words and my organizing, and having folks stare at me while I try to sort it all out.

My mind is quiet in that regard. And I wouldn't say I'm sad, exactly, just terribly embarrassed like I mentioned before. But you asked about feeling confused, or folks finding things strange, and... well, there is one other thing that's been bothering me lately, now that you bring it up. It makes me feel terribly confused, Doctor, because in my head I mean to answer straight, but what comes out is just a whole mess of beans and hymns and garden flowers, and it just leaves everybody scratching their heads.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your mood, energy, or interest in things you used to enjoy, like church activities or gardening, over the past few weeks or months?\n\nPatient: Well, my energy is just fine, Doctor, and my mood... well, I wouldn't say I'm depressed or anything like that. I was telling people to put the green beans with the chalk! \n\nAnd folks... well, people get uncomfortable. I can see it in their eyes, just like when my words run away from me. And then poor Betty or Mrs. Higgins ends up having to stay late and completely redo what I was supposed to handle. Well now, Doctor, that's a mighty fine question, and I wish I had a simple little answer to hand right over to you, but... well, to tell you the honest truth, I really couldn't say one way or the other. I just don't know. 

You see, it’s not like a leaky pipe under the kitchen sink where you can just sit there and watch the drip get faster and faster until you’ve got a puddle ruining the good linoleum. It’s... well, it’s harder to measure than that. Some days I wake up, and the sun is shining right through those yellow gingham curtains I sewed for the kitchen window back in, oh, it must have been 2004, and I go about my business making my morning oatmeal with just a little dash of cinnamon and a splash of milk, and everything is just fine. My thoughts are as straight and neat as a freshly hoed row of radishes, and I don't have a single bit of trouble. 

But then other days... well, it just sneaks up on me. Like just last Thursday, I was down at the Piggly Wiggly, and I was trying to explain to the checkout girl—the sweet one with the curly red hair who always wears that little silver locket, she's always so patient with me—I was just trying to tell her I needed her to double-bag the heavy things because the paper handles tear so easily. And instead, I started going on and on about the windshield wipers on a John Deere tractor! 

Now, was that worse than what happened with Mrs. Higgins and the blue bedsheets back in the spring? I just don't rightly know. It feels like it’s just the same old foolishness, popping up whenever it pleases. It doesn't feel like it's a heavier burden today than it was a few months ago, but it certainly hasn't packed its bags and left, either. It just comes and goes, ruining my sentences or making a mess of my sorting, and then leaves me standing there feeling like a prize turkey. He gave me one of those plastic organizers, you know the ones, with the days of the week printed on 'em in big black letters, so I never miss a day. Sunday, Monday, right on down the line. I keep it right next to the toaster so I see it when I make my morning tea. But he hasn't changed it, hasn't added anything new at all. I don't take anything else. I certainly don't drink any alcohol or take any kind of bad substances—my father smoked a pipe when I was little and the smell of it was enough to put me off even tobacco for my whole life. \n\nSo no, no new medicines, no sicknesses, no falling down. I'm just healthy as a horse, which makes it all the more confounding why my arm would just stick up in the air over that macaroni salad like that. It just doesn't make a single lick of sense to me, Doctor, it really doesn't.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any other changes lately, like hearing or seeing things that others don't, having thoughts or beliefs that others find strange, or feeling unusually sad, anxious, or confused?\n\nPatient: Well, I certainly don't see anything that isn't there, thank the Lord, and I don't hear any voices or anything spooky like that. My mind is quiet in that regard. And I wouldn't say I'm sad, exactly, just terribly embarrassed like I mentioned before. But you asked about feeling confused, or folks finding things strange, and... well, there is one other thing that's been bothering me lately, now that you bring it up. I knew exactly what I wanted to say about the yarn I bought at the five-and-dime. \n\nBut when I opened my mouth, my words just... they just ran off. They ran off completely. Well now, I suppose I could give that a try, Doctor. If you think having me do a little quiz is going to help figure out why my tongue gets all tangled up when I'm trying to talk to folks, then I am more than happy to oblige.

I just... my hands just kept moving, smoothing 'em down, over and over, and my brain was just completely out to pasture. I didn't even feel upset or worried until I sort of came to my senses and saw that whole line of folks backed up to the double doors staring at me like I'd grown a second head. That's when the worry hits, Doctor, the sheer embarrassment of it all, having everybody looking at you like you're crazy. But during the actual doing of it? No, no thoughts at all. Just completely frozen up like a deer in the headlights, without a single reason why.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any recent medical illnesses, head injuries, neurological problems, or new medications/substances around the time these episodes started?\n\nPatient: Well, no, Doctor. I've been blessed with pretty sturdy health, praise the Lord. I haven't had so much as a sniffle lately, let alone any big sicknesses. I know some folks my age are always in and out of the doctor's office, falling down and hitting their heads and what have you. Like my neighbor, Mr. Abernathy, he took a tumble off his porch steps just last November and had a terrible bump on his head, but me? No, I'm real careful. I always hold onto the handrail when I go down the steps to the basement to fetch my canning jars. Never hit my head, never had any of those... well, you called them neurological things. He gave me one of those plastic organizers, you know the ones, with the days of the week printed on 'em in big black letters, so I never miss a day. Sunday, Monday, right on down the line. I keep it right next to the toaster so I see it when I make my morning tea. But he hasn't changed it, hasn't added anything new at all. I don't take anything else. My mind is quiet in that regard. And I wouldn't say I'm sad, exactly, just terribly embarrassed like I mentioned before. I still love my garden, I really do. Just being out there with the dirt and the Lord's earth, it's a real comfort to me. Completely scramble them up in my head. \n\nLike just a few weeks ago, I was supposed to be in charge of organizing the donation boxes for the winter drive—putting the canned goods in one pile and the dry goods in another, making sure the expiration dates were good, just simple things I've done a hundred times. I remembered to ask him how she was doing because he'd told me way back in the spring that she was due in late October, and I kept that right up here in my head all those months. \n\nSo no, I don't forget what folks tell me. It's just... well, like I said, it's the getting my own words out straight and scrambling up the sorting boxes that's the problem. But remembering the actual information? No, my mind holds onto all that just as clear as a bell.\n\nDoctor: Thinking back, when did you first start noticing these problems—the freezing spells, the mixed-up words, and the trouble organizing things—did they come on suddenly over a few days or weeks, or have they been slowly getting worse over many months or even years?\n\nPatient: Well now, let me sit and chew on that for a second, Doctor. You know, time has a funny way of slipping by when you get to be my age, it just runs right through your fingers like dry potting soil. But no, it certainly wasn't an overnight thing. I didn't just wake up on a Tuesday morning with my tongue all tied in knots and my hands putting the canned corn in with the choir robes. But it hasn't been years and years, either, thank goodness. \n\nIf I really trace it back... back to when folks first started getting that confused look on their faces, and when I first started realizing my words were just running clean away from me... I'd say it's been right about six months now. Yes, half a year. I know that for a fact because it was right around the time we were getting ready for the Easter sunrise service. We had that terrible late frost that just about ruined all the dogwood blooms, and I was out in the front yard trying to cover my delicate azaleas with some old bedsheets—the blue striped ones my sister Martha gave me back in the late nineties, they're terribly worn at the hems now but they do the trick for the frost. \n\nAnyway, Mrs. Higgins had walked over to the fence to ask if I'd ordered the palm fronds for Palm Sunday. That was the very first time she gave me that squinty, upside-down-map look I was telling you about. \n\nSo yes, all this odd behavior, the muddling things up at the church and the hard-to-follow talking... it hasn't been forever, but it’s been noticeable for about the past six months now. I just don't know. \n\nYou see, it’s not like a leaky pipe under the kitchen sink where you can just sit there and watch the drip get faster and faster until you’ve got a puddle ruining the good linoleum. It’s... well, it’s harder to measure than that. Some days I wake up, and the sun is shining right through those yellow gingham curtains I sewed for the kitchen window back in, oh, it must have been 2004, and I go about my business making my morning oatmeal with just a little dash of cinnamon and a splash of milk, and everything is just fine. My thoughts are as straight and neat as a freshly hoed row of radishes, and I don't have a single bit of trouble. \n\nBut then other days... well, it just sneaks up on me. Like just last Thursday, I was down at the Piggly Wiggly, and I was trying to explain to the checkout girl—the sweet one with the curly red hair who always wears that little silver locket, she's always so patient with me—I was just trying to tell her I needed her to double-bag the heavy things because the paper handles tear so easily. And instead, I started going on and on about the windshield wipers on a John Deere tractor! \n\nNow, was that worse than what happened with Mrs. Higgins and the blue bedsheets back in the spring? I just don't rightly know. It feels like it’s just the same old foolishness, popping up whenever it pleases. It doesn't feel like it's a heavier burden today than it was a few months ago, but it certainly hasn't packed its bags and left, either. It just comes and goes, ruining my sentences or making a mess of my sorting, and then leaves me standing there feeling like a prize turkey. So I really couldn't tell you if it's sliding downhill or just parked right there in the driveway. I just know it's there.\n\nDoctor: Besides the trouble finding words and organizing tasks, have you noticed any new difficulty with everyday things like dressing yourself, cooking, driving, or recognizing familiar people or places?\n\nPatient: Oh heavens no, Doctor, nothing like that at all. I am fully capable of taking care of myself, thank the good Lord. Why, just this morning... well, I always lay my clothes out the night before, you see. It's a habit my mother instilled in me way back when we lived out on the old farm and had to be up before the sun to collect the eggs. I still do it to this very day. Last night, I picked out my lavender blouse with the little pearl snaps—the one my niece got me from a catalog for my sixty-fifth birthday, it washes beautifully—and I didn't have a single bit of trouble getting my arms in the sleeves or fastening those tiny little snaps this morning. My hands work just fine for dressing, and I always make sure I look presentable before I step foot out the door. \n\nAnd cooking? Oh, my goodness, if I couldn't cook, I don't know what I'd do with myself! I'm still making all my regular meals, three times a day. Just yesterday I put together a beautiful chuck roast with carrots and those little waxy red potatoes, simmering it slow in my heavy cast-iron Dutch oven all afternoon. I know exactly how much salt and pepper to put in, and I certainly don't forget to turn the stove off. I've never once burned a pan or forgotten the steps to make my buttermilk biscuits. I can still pinch the dough just right.\n\nAs for the driving... well, I still have my 1998 Buick Century. It’s that lovely champagne color, you know the one? I have to tell you, I never was much for the higher mathematics. I actually left school right in the middle of the eighth grade, you see. I certainly don't drink any alcohol or take any kind of bad substances—my father smoked a pipe when I was little and the smell of it was enough to put me off even tobacco for my whole life. \n\nSo no, no new medicines, no sicknesses, no falling down. I'm just healthy as a horse, which makes it all the more confounding why my arm would just stick up in the air over that macaroni salad like that. My mind is quiet in that regard. And I wouldn't say I'm sad, exactly, just terribly embarrassed like I mentioned before. Completely scramble them up in my head. \n\nLike just a few weeks ago, I was supposed to be in charge of organizing the donation boxes for the winter drive—putting the canned goods in one pile and the dry goods in another, making sure the expiration dates were good, just simple things I've done a hundred times. I was telling people to put the green beans with the chalk! \n\nAnd folks... well, people get uncomfortable. I can see it in their eyes, just like when my words run away from me. And then poor Betty or Mrs. Higgins ends up having to stay late and completely redo what I was supposed to handle. I'd say it's been right about six months now. Yes, half a year. I know that for a fact because it was right around the time we were getting ready for the Easter sunrise service. We had that terrible late frost that just about ruined all the dogwood blooms, and I was out in the front yard trying to cover my delicate azaleas with some old bedsheets—the blue striped ones my sister Martha gave me back in the late nineties, they're terribly worn at the hems now but they do the trick for the frost. \n\nAnyway, Mrs. Higgins had walked over to the fence to ask if I'd ordered the palm fronds for Palm Sunday. And I remember standing there, holding a corner of that blue sheet, and I opened my mouth to tell her I'd already called the florist down on Main Street. But out came this whole long string of nonsense about the recipe for my paprika deviled eggs and the price of the white shoe polish I use on my Sunday heels! That was the very first time she gave me that squinty, upside-down-map look I was telling you about. \n\nSo yes, all this odd behavior, the muddling things up at the church and the hard-to-follow talking... it hasn't been forever, but it’s been noticeable for about the past six months now. Six months of just... well, just making a mess of my words and my organizing, and having folks stare at me while I try to sort it all out.\n\nDoctor: Over these past six months, would you say the trouble finding the right words and keeping your plans straight has been gradually getting worse, or has it stayed about the same since it first started?\n\nPatient: Well now, Doctor, that's a mighty fine question, and I wish I had a simple little answer to hand right over to you, but... well, to tell you the honest truth, I really couldn't say one way or the other. I just don't know. \n\nYou see, it’s not like a leaky pipe under the kitchen sink where you can just sit there and watch the drip get faster and faster until you’ve got a puddle ruining the good linoleum. It’s... well, it’s harder to measure than that. Some days I wake up, and the sun is shining right through those yellow gingham curtains I sewed for the kitchen window back in, oh, it must have been 2004, and I go about my business making my morning oatmeal with just a little dash of cinnamon and a splash of milk, and everything is just fine. My thoughts are as straight and neat as a freshly hoed row of radishes, and I don't have a single bit of trouble. \n\nBut then other days... well, it just sneaks up on me. Like just last Thursday, I was down at the Piggly Wiggly, and I was trying to explain to the checkout girl—the sweet one with the curly red hair who always wears that little silver locket, she's always so patient with me—I was just trying to tell her I needed her to double-bag the heavy things because the paper handles tear so easily. And instead, I started going on and on about the windshield wipers on a John Deere tractor! \n\nNow, was that worse than what happened with Mrs. Higgins and the blue bedsheets back in the spring? I just don't rightly know. It feels like it’s just the same old foolishness, popping up whenever it pleases. It doesn't feel like it's a heavier burden today than it was a few months ago, but it certainly hasn't packed its bags and left, either. It just comes and goes, ruining my sentences or making a mess of my sorting, and then leaves me standing there feeling like a prize turkey. So I really couldn't tell you if it's sliding downhill or just parked right there in the driveway. I just know it's there.\n\nDoctor: Besides the trouble finding words and organizing tasks, have you noticed any new difficulty with everyday things like dressing yourself, cooking, driving, or recognizing familiar people or places?\n\nPatient: Oh heavens no, Doctor, nothing like that at all. I am fully capable of taking care of myself, thank the good Lord. Why, just this morning... well, I always lay my clothes out the night before, you see. It's a habit my mother instilled in me way back when we lived out on the old farm and had to be up before the sun to collect the eggs. I still do it to this very day. Last night, I picked out my lavender blouse with the little pearl snaps—the one my niece got me from a catalog for my sixty-fifth birthday, it washes beautifully—and I didn't have a single bit of trouble getting my arms in the sleeves or fastening those tiny little snaps this morning. My hands work just fine for dressing, and I always make sure I look presentable before I step foot out the door. \n\nAnd cooking? Oh, my goodness, if I couldn't cook, I don't know what I'd do with myself! I'm still making all my regular meals, three times a day. Just yesterday I put together a beautiful chuck roast with carrots and those little waxy red potatoes, simmering it slow in my heavy cast-iron Dutch oven all afternoon. I know exactly how much salt and pepper to put in, and I certainly don't forget to turn the stove off. I've never once burned a pan or forgotten the steps to make my buttermilk biscuits. I can still pinch the dough just right.\n\nAs for the driving... well, I still have my 1998 Buick Century. It’s that lovely champagne color, you know the one? It’s got quite a few miles on it, but I keep it running smooth, take it in for its oil changes right on schedule. I drive myself down to the grocery store, over to the church fellowship hall, and to my hair appointments with Brenda on Thursday mornings. I know every turn, every stop sign, and every single pothole on County Road 9. I don't get lost, not ever. \n\nAnd recognizing folks? Well, I'd have to be blind as a bat not to know who I'm looking at! I know every face in this town. If I see Sarah Jenkins down at the pharmacy, I know right away it's Sarah, even if she did just dye her hair that awful brassy blonde color that washes her out terribly. I know the streets, I know my friends, I know my own house inside and out. So no, Doctor, it's really just the... the talking nonsense out of nowhere and the organizing the church papers that gets me all turned around. Every other part of my day is just as normal as blueberry pie.\n\nDoctor: Would you be willing to try a few quick memory and thinking exercises with me right now, like naming today's date, repeating a short list of words back to me, or counting backwards from 100 by sevens?\n\nPatient: Well now, I suppose I could give that a try, Doctor. If you think having me do a little quiz is going to help figure out why my tongue gets all tangled up when I'm trying to talk to folks, then I am more than happy to oblige. \n\nCounting backwards by sevens, though... oh my, that sounds like a bit of a tall order! I have to tell you, I never was much for the higher mathematics. I actually left school right in the middle of the eighth grade, you see. It was back when we lived out in Oakhaven, and my mother had just had my youngest brother, Thomas—he was a terribly sickly baby, always colicky and needing to be walked up and down the hall at all hours of the night, just wailing like a little siren. So my father sat me down at the kitchen table one evening, right after supper, and said I needed to trade my schoolbooks for a wooden spoon and a laundry washboard to help keep the house running. And that’s exactly what I did, so I never got to the fancy algebra or the complicated ciphering. But I can count my change at the grocery store just fine, down to the very last penny, I'll have you know! \n\nAnd as for repeating a list of words back to you... well, that sounds an awful lot like that game we used to play at the church picnics. Telephone, I think the children called it? Where you whisper a secret into one person's ear, and they pass it down the line, and by the time it gets to the end, \"purple petunias\" turns into \"turtle balloons\" or some such nonsense! We had a good laugh over that back in... oh, it must have been the summer of '82, over at Centennial Park. The mosquitoes were just terrible that year, I remember I had to rub apple cider vinegar all over my ankles just to sit on the picnic blanket without getting eaten alive. \n\nBut yes, yes, I am more than willing to do your little exercises. I might need a second to think on the exact date, seeing as how the days sort of bleed together when you don't have to punch a time clock or catch a school bus anymore, but I will certainly do my level best for you. You just go right ahead and tell me what you want me to do first, Doctor. I'm ready whenever you are.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me today's exact date, including the month, day, and year?\n\nPatient: Oh my, put right on the spot! Well, let me just think on that for a minute, Doctor. You see, I usually have that big wall calendar right by the telephone in the kitchen—the one the local pharmacy gives out for free every December. This year's has the most lovely pictures of old covered bridges from all across the country, just beautiful scenes with the autumn leaves and the snow. I always make sure to circle the important days in red ink, like my hair appointments with Brenda or when the electric bill is due, so I don't miss a single thing. \n\nBut sitting here in this office, without my calendar to look at... well, goodness. I know it's... well, the days just fly by so fast when you aren't waiting on a Friday paycheck or sending kids off on the school bus, like I was saying before. Is it the middle of the month already? I'm afraid I just couldn't pull the exact month and day out of my hat for you right this second. And the year... well, sometimes I still catch myself writing the old year on my checks at the grocery store, just out of pure habit! It takes me until spring to get my hand used to the new numbers. \n\nSo to give you the exact month, day, and year all together right now... no, it's just slipped right out of my mind like water through a colander. I know it's a weekday, because the garbage men always come clattering down our alley on Tuesdays and that wasn't today, but that exact date? No, I just don't rightly know it off the top of my head.\n\nDoctor: During one of these freezing spells, if someone gently tried to move your arm or guide you to put the spoon down, did your arm resist and stay stiff, or did it move easily and stay in whatever new position they placed it?\n\nPatient: Well now, you see, that's exactly the sort of thing that brought me in here to see you in the first place, Doctor. It's just been worrying me half to death. I came in because, well, at church I keep doing these odd things lately, and it's getting to be quite a spectacle. \n\nWe always have these lovely potluck dinners down in the fellowship hall on the first Sunday of the month—everyone brings a dish, and we set them all out on those long folding tables. But lately, I'll be standing right by the potluck table, right where all the hot casseroles are, and I'll pick up the serving spoon to get myself a scoop of macaroni or what have you, and I'll just end up holding the serving spoon up in the air and not moving at all. I just freeze right up, like a statue in the park! \n\nNow, as to whether my arm is stiff or if it moves easily when someone tries to guide it down... oh heavens, I don't rightly know for sure. When I get stuck like that, my mind is just sort of blank, or I'm so caught up that I don't even realize what my own limbs are doing until somebody says, \"Mildred, are you alright?\" I don't remember fighting anybody on it, but I couldn't tell you if my arm stayed where they put it, because I'm just so mortified once I realize I've been standing there holding up the line. \n\nAnd it's not just the serving spoons, either. Sometimes I'll be at the end of the table where they keep the cutlery, and I'll find myself folding the exact same stack of paper napkins over and over again. Just creasing them, smoothing them out, and folding them right back up, over and over, while a whole line of folks are standing there holding their little paper plates, just waiting on me to move along so they can get their supper. It's terribly embarrassing, Doctor, doing these odd things out of nowhere when I'm just trying to have a nice Sunday meal with my friends. That's really why I knew I had to come see you, because I just can't be holding up the buffet line every month like that!\n\nDoctor: Have your family or friends noticed any changes in your personality or behavior lately—like acting unusually impulsive, saying or doing things that seem out of character, or seeming less interested in things socially—apart from the freezing spells and word mix-ups?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think on that... impulsive? Oh heavens, no. I have never been one to just jump into things without looking, Doctor. Why, my late husband, Arthur, rest his soul, used to say I was the most predictable woman in the whole county! I'm the sort of person who writes out my grocery list based on the exact aisle layout at the store so I don't have to backtrack, you see. I like things orderly and planned out. So nobody in my family or at the church has said a single peep about me acting out of character or doing wild things, no sir. \n\nAnd as for not being interested in my social activities... well, my goodness, I am just as busy as a bee! I haven't missed a Tuesday morning coffee group with the ladies in... oh, it must be fifteen years now. Well, except for that time I had a terrible bout of the shingles back in '98, which was just dreadful, let me tell you—I had to use calamine lotion by the gallon and couldn't bear to wear anything but my loosest cotton housecoat for three solid weeks. But other than that, no, I still absolutely love visiting with folks. \n\nJust this past Wednesday, my friend Martha—she's the one who organizes the church rummage sale every spring, you know, a very particular woman, always wants the donated sweaters folded just so and color-coordinated—she called me up on the telephone and we talked for near on an hour about the new choir director and his rather... vibrant taste in neckties. So I am still very much enjoying my social time and keeping up with everyone's news. So I really couldn't tell you if it's sliding downhill or just parked right there in the driveway. Last night, I picked out my lavender blouse with the little pearl snaps—the one my niece got me from a catalog for my sixty-fifth birthday, it washes beautifully—and I didn't have a single bit of trouble getting my arms in the sleeves or fastening those tiny little snaps this morning. I know exactly how much salt and pepper to put in, and I certainly don't forget to turn the stove off. I've never once burned a pan or forgotten the steps to make my buttermilk biscuits. I can still pinch the dough just right.\n\nAs for the driving... well, I still have my 1998 Buick Century. It’s that lovely champagne color, you know the one? It’s got quite a few miles on it, but I keep it running smooth, take it in for its oil changes right on schedule.
